title: Better Data Labelling with EMBLEM (and how that Impacts Defect Prediction)

edges.target: EMBLEM / FASTREAD active learner (Yu, Kraft & Menzies)
edges.ref: [114] Z. Yu, N. A. Kraft, and T Menzies. Finding better active learners for faster literature reviews. EMSE, 2018.
edges.evidence: we adopted an active learning framework developed for reading research papers in SE literatures [112], [114], [115], [116], called EMBLEM

edges.target: EMBLEM parameter settings {N1=4000,N2=1,N3=30,N4=95%} (Yu et al.)
edges.ref: [114] Z. Yu, N. A. Kraft, and T Menzies. Finding better active learners for faster literature reviews. EMSE, 2018.
edges.evidence: Those decisions where made by Yu et al. [114] after exploring 32 different kinds of active learners ... obtained using Yu et al.'s original decisions [114], [116] without extensive tuning.

edges.target: FAST2 (Yu & Menzies)
edges.ref: [116] Z. Yu and T. Menzies. Fast2: An intelligent assistant for finding relevant papers. Expert Systems with Applications, 2019.
edges.evidence: All those aforementioned tactics are built into EMBLEM [114], [116], the active learner used for this work.

edges.target: Wallace's aggressive undersampling
edges.ref: [103] B. C Wallace, T. A Trikalinos, J. Lau, C. Brodley, C. H Schmid. Semi-automated screening of biomedical citations for systematic reviews. 2010
edges.evidence: EMBLEM trains further using certainty sampling and Wallace's "aggressive undersampling" [103] that culls majority class examples closest to the decision boundary.

edges.target: Cormack & Grossman continuous active learning (TAR state of the art)
edges.ref: [22] G. V Cormack and M. R Grossman. Autonomy and reliability of continuous active learning for technology-assisted review. CoRR, 2015.
edges.evidence: They report that, using the above requirements, EMBLEM found more relevant items faster than the previously reported state-of-the-art in incremental text mining retrieval [22], [102].

edges.target: Wallace et al. active learning for citation screening
edges.ref: [102] B. C. Wallace, K. Small, C. E. Brodley, and T. A. Trikalinos. Active learning for biomedical citation screening. In 16th SIGKDD, 2010.
edges.evidence: EMBLEM found more relevant items faster than the previously reported state-of-the-art in incremental text mining retrieval [22], [102].

edges.target: Ros et al. remaining-relevant estimator
edges.ref: [85] R. Ros, E. Bjarnason, P. Runeson. A machine learning approach for semi-automated search and selection in literature studies. EASE 2017
edges.evidence: the N4 estimator converged much faster and obtained better estimates that other prominent estimators from the text mining literature [23], [85], [100].

edges.target: EMBLEM applied to vulnerability inspection (Yu et al.)
edges.ref: [117] Z. Yu, C. Theisen, L. Williams, and T. Menzies. Improving vulnerability inspection efficiency using active learning. TSE, 2019.
edges.evidence: It has been proofed to be effective not only in reading research papers, but also in inspecting software security vulnerabilities [117], finding self-admitted technical debt [30], and test case prioritization [113].

edges.target: Commit.Guru (Rosen, Grawi & Shihab) - data collection + SZZ implementation
edges.ref: [86] C. Rosen, B. Grawi, and E. Shihab. Commit guru: Analytics and risk prediction of software commits. ESEC/FSE 2015, 2015.
edges.evidence: For this analysis, we used Commit.Guru tool [86]. This tool was used since Commit.Guru supports web-scale data collection from on-line Github projects.

edges.target: Commit.Guru keyword labelling (baseline)
edges.ref: [86] C. Rosen, B. Grawi, and E. Shihab. Commit guru: Analytics and risk prediction of software commits. ESEC/FSE 2015, 2015.
edges.evidence: Comparing EMBLEM vs Keywords (from Commit.Guru) for bug-fixing commits identification performance ... Keywords labelling result in lower recall and higher false alarms

edges.target: Keyword taxonomy for commit labelling (Hindle, German & Holt)
edges.ref: [41] A. Hindle, D. M. German, and R. Holt. What do large commits tell us?: A taxonomical study of large commits. MSR, 2008.
edges.evidence: This paper argues against using keywords like these as a method for labelling a commit as "buggy". Keywords from [41].

edges.target: SZZ algorithm (Sliwerski, Zimmermann & Zeller)
edges.ref: [91] Jacek Sliwerski, Thomas Zimmermann, and Andreas Zeller. When do changes induce fixes? SIGSOFT Softw. Eng. Notes, 2005.
edges.evidence: we used Sliwerski, Zimmermann, and Zeller's SZZ's algorithm [26], [52], [91] to work back in time ... (and the SZZ implementation we used here came from Commit.Guru).

edges.target: SZZ usage count (Rodriguez-Perez et al.)
edges.ref: [84] G. Rodriguez, G. Robles, J. Gonzalez-Barahona. Reproducibility and credibility in empirical SE: ... the szz algorithm. IST 2018
edges.evidence: Rodrguez-Perez et al. [84] report that at least 187 papers have also used SZZ in the same way as these experiments of this paper.

edges.target: Kamei et al. 14 change-level JIT features + release-based train/test protocol
edges.ref: [48] Y. Kamei, E. Shihab, B. Adams, A. E. Hassan, A. Mockus, A. Sinha, N. Ubayashi. A large-scale empirical study of just-in-time quality assurance. T
edges.evidence: 14 independent commit-level features, collected by Commit.Guru. [48]. ... This method is applied and endorsed through previous studies that solely using automating keyword [17], [48], [75], [86].

edges.target: Eclipse JDT and Eclipse Platform JIT defect data (Kamei et al.)
edges.ref: [48] Y. Kamei, E. Shihab, B. Adams, A. E. Hassan, A. Mockus, A. Sinha, N. Ubayashi. A large-scale empirical study of just-in-time quality assurance. T
edges.evidence: we applied EMBLEM to a sample of standard large-scale SE projects, Eclipse JDT (E.JDT) and Eclipse Platform (E.PLATFORM). We used this data since it has previously been used in several prior papers [48], [109].

edges.target: Scott-Knott ranking (Mittas & Angelis)
edges.ref: [67] N. Mittas and L. Angelis. Ranking and clustering software cost estimation models through a multiple comparisons algorithm. TSE, 2013.
edges.evidence: This study ranks treatments using the Scott-Knott procedure recommended by Mittas & Angelis in their 2013 IEEE TSE paper [67].

edges.target: Non-parametric bootstrap (Efron & Tibshirani)
edges.ref: [28] B. Efron and R. J Tibshirani. An introduction to the bootstrap. Mono. Stat. Appl. Probab. London, 1994.
edges.evidence: our hypothesis test H was a conjunction of the A12 effect size test of and non-parametric bootstrap sampling ... see Efron & Tibshirani [28, p220-223].

edges.target: Vargha-Delaney A12 effect size (as endorsed by Arcuri & Briand)
edges.ref: [7] A. Arcuri and L. Briand. A practical guide for using statistical tests to assess randomized algorithms in software engineering. In ICSE, 2011.
edges.evidence: Vargha and Delaney's non-parametric A12 effect size test was endorsed by Arcuri and Briand [7]. ... not a "small" effect (A12 >= 0.6).

edges.target: Effect-size rule (Kampenes et al.)
edges.ref: [49] V. B. Kampenes, T. Dyba, J. E. Hannay, and D. I. K. Sjoberg. A systematic review of effect size in software engineering experiments. IST, 2007.
edges.evidence: For a justification of the use of effect size tests see Kampenes [49] who warn that even if a hypothesis test declares two populations to be "significantly" different, then that result is misleading

edges.target: Ghotra et al. learner ranking (32 defect predictors)
edges.ref: [36] B. Ghotra, S. McIntosh, A. E. Hassan. Revisiting the impact of classification techniques on the performance of defect prediction models. ICSE 201
edges.evidence: we use the Ghotra et al. ICSE paper that grouped 32 defect predictors into different ranks (see Table 9 of [36]). For this study, we used Random Forests+J48 and Logistic Regression

edges.target: FFTs for defect prediction (Chen et al.)
edges.ref: [18] D. Chen, W. Fu, R. Krishna, and T. Menzies. Applications of psychological science for actionable analytics. In FSE, 2018.
edges.evidence: we use one method reported very recently at FSE'19 (FFTs, describe below) ... Chen et al. [18] reported that this method performs dramatically better than many prior results seen at recent ICSE conferences

edges.target: Fast and Frugal Trees (Martignon et al.)
edges.ref: [61] L. Martignon, K. V Katsikopoulos, J. K Woike. Categorization with limited resources: A family of simple heuristics. J. Math. Psych. 2008
edges.evidence: One FFT (in a FFTs model) is a decision tree made as a binary tree where all internal nodes have one leaf node with a guard condition leading to a classification decision [61].

edges.target: Random Forests (Breiman)
edges.ref: [15] L. Breiman. Random forests. Machine Learning, 2001.
edges.evidence: our Random Forests builds many trees, each time using different subsets of the data rows R and columns C ... the conclusions are determined (say) a majority vote across all the trees [15].

edges.target: Logistic Regression (Witten, Frank & Hall)
edges.ref: [105] I. H. Witten, E. Frank, and M. A. Hall. Data Mining: Practical Machine Learning Tools and Techniques. Morgan Kaufmann, 3rd edition, 2011.
edges.evidence: Logistic Regresion maps t into the range 0..1 using u = 1/(1 + e^-t) [105].

edges.target: SMO SVM (Zeng et al.)
edges.ref: [118] Z. Q. Zeng, H. B. Yu, H. R. Xu, Y. Q. Xie, J. Gao. Fast training support vector machines using parallel sequential minimal optimization. ISKE 20
edges.evidence: following the results of Ghotra et al. [36], the Sequential Minimal Optimization (SMO) SVM technique is used. SMO analytically solves the large Quadratic Programming (QP) optimization problem [118].

edges.target: Tuned SMOTE (Agrawal & Menzies)
edges.ref: [3] A. Agrawal and T. Menzies. Is better data better than better data miners?: on the benefits of tuning smote for defect prediction. IST 2018
edges.evidence: SMOTE can be improved by some local tuning [3], [12]. We do not use such local tuning since recently is has been shown that such tunings are outperformed by FFTs

edges.target: G-score for imbalanced data (Zhang & Zhang; Shatnawi)
edges.ref: [119] H. Zhang and X. Zhang. Comments on "data mining static code attributes to learn defect predictors". TSE, 2007.
edges.evidence: The G-score is the harmonic mean between recall and the compliment of the false alarm rate ... recommended for data sets like ours where some of the test samples have imbalanced class distributions [89], [119].

edges.target: Deprecating precision/accuracy for rare-class data (Menzies et al.)
edges.ref: [63] T. Menzies, A. Dekhtyar, J. Distefano, J. Greenwald. Problems with precision: A response to "comments on 'data mining static code attributes'". T
edges.evidence: we deprecate the use of precision and accuracy since these can be misleading for data sets where the target class is somewhat rare [63]

edges.target: Popt20 / 20-80 rule (Ostrand, Weyuker & Bell)
edges.ref: [77] T. J Ostrand, E. J Weyuker, and R. M Bell. Where the bugs are. In ACM SIGSOFT Software Engineering Notes, 2004.
edges.evidence: We also evaluate our results using the 20/80 rule from Ostrand et al. [77]. They say a "good" defect predictor selects the 20% of files containing 80% of the defects

edges.target: GitHub project sanity checks (Kalliamvakou et al.)
edges.ref: [45] E. Kalliamvakou, G. Gousios, K. Blincoe, L. Singer, D. German, and D. Damian. The promises and perils of mining github. In MSR, 2014.
edges.evidence: following the advice of Kalliamvakou et al. [45], we used the sanity checks of Table 5b to prune these to 59 projects.

edges.target: Nine-stage ML workflow (Amershi et al., Microsoft)
edges.ref: [5] S. Amershi, A. Begel, C. Bird, R. DeLine, H. Gall, E. Kamar, N. Nagappan, B. Nushi, T. Zimmermann. Software engineering for machine learning. ICSE
edges.evidence: As shown in Figure 1, there are at least nine separate stages that must be completed before that goal be reached [5]. ... They are mapped to our problem as:

edges.target: SATD labelling time: 33,093 comments in ~95 hours (Maldonado & Shihab)
edges.ref: [60] E. da S Maldonado and E. Shihab. Detecting and quantifying different types of self-admitted technical debt. In 2015 MTD, 2015.
edges.evidence: classifying 33,093 comments as "SATD" from five open source projects took approximately 95 hours by a single person; i.e. 10.3 seconds per comment. Using that information, we calculated

edges.target: Linkster labelling rate ~500 commits/day (Bird et al.)
edges.ref: [9] A. Bachmann, C. Bird, F. Rahman, P. Devanbu, and A. Bernstein. The missing links: Bugs and bug-fix commits. In FSE, 2010.
edges.evidence: Linkster helps researchers manually label around 500 commits within a working day ... a large scale Linkster-style analysis would be too costly in real-world scenarios.

edges.target: ReLink (Wu et al.)
edges.ref: [106] R. Wu, H. Zhang, S. Kim, and S. Cheung. Relink: Recovering links between bugs and changes. ESEC/FSE, 2011.
edges.evidence: Their methods are not valid and applicable unless the labelling is correct in the first place (which needs EMBLEM).

edges.target: Linux bug-fixing patch identification via PU-learning + SVM (Tian, Lawall & Lo)
edges.ref: [93] Y. Tian, J. Lawall, and D. Lo. Identifying linux bug fixing patches. ICSE, 2012.
edges.evidence: As to Relink and the methods of Lo et al., these approaches assume the existence of some pre-labelled examples.

edges.target: 50% crowdworker cull rate (Chen, Stolee & Menzies)
edges.ref: [19] D. Chen, K. T. Stolee, and T. Menzies. Replication can improve prior results: A github study of pull request acceptance. In ICPC, 2019.
edges.evidence: (d) a 50% "cull rate" of crowd workers ... Such a 50% "cull rate" is common practice in crowdsourcincg [19]

edges.target: Ad hoc keyword usage critique (Vasilescu et al.)
edges.ref: [98] B. Vasilescu, Y. Yu, H. Wang, P. Devanbu, V. Filkov. Quality and productivity outcomes relating to continuous integration in github. FSE 2015
edges.evidence: Vasilescu et al. [97], [98] notes that these keywords are used in somewhat ad hoc manner (researchers peek at a few results, then tinker with regular expressions

edges.target: Practitioner survey: >90% willing to adopt defect prediction (Wan et al.)
edges.ref: [104] Z. Wan, X. Xia, A. E. Hassan, D. Lo, J. Yin, and X. Yang. Perceptions, expectations, & challenges in defect prediction. TSE, 2018.
edges.evidence: In a survey of 395 practitioners from 33 countries and five continents, Wan et al. [104] found that over 90% of the respondents were willing to adopt defect prediction

edges.target: Static bug finders vs statistical prediction equivalence (Rahman et al.)
edges.ref: [82] F. Rahman, S. Khatri, E. T Barr, and P. Devanbu. Comparing static bug finders and statistical prediction. In ICSE. ACM, 2014.
edges.evidence: Rahman et al. [82] compared (a) static code analysis tools FindBugs, Jlint, and PMD with (b) defect predictors ... No significant differences in cost-effectiveness were observed.

edges.target: Process metrics matter (Rahman & Devanbu)
edges.ref: [81] F. Rahman and P. Devanbu. How, and why, process metrics are better. In ICSE, 2013.
edges.evidence: Herslab [94] and Devanbu [81] argue convincingly that it is important to collect information about (a) the humans changing the code as (b) the code itself.

not_reuse_examples: [43] Jureczko & Madeyski - cited only as an example of widely reused shared data (the 177-paper count is the authors' own Google Scholar search), not used here.
[1] Agrawal et al. DODGE and [109] Yang et al. deep belief network - mentioned only as future-work avenues, not run or compared.

[83],[59],[11],[6],[37],[87],[35],[79],[53] - citations describing the nine studied computational-science software systems; the commit data was mined fresh by the authors via Commit.Guru, so these are subject descriptions, not reused datasets.
[104]-style motivation refs such as [66] Misirli, [51] Kim REMI, [33] Fu et al. - background on the value of defect prediction; only the most premise-like ones were kept.
notes: Empirical JIT defect-prediction paper (arXiv 1905.01719v3, TSE-style); heavy self-reuse of the authors' FASTREAD/EMBLEM active learner; keyword labelling via Commit.Guru is the refuted baseline; Table 13 is a self-replication on Eclipse data, not a re-run of a prior study.
